lesson.title: The SCH Bridge
lesson.subtitle: English sh is Dutch sch — one sound, three letters

hook.title: One Sound, Three Letters
hook.content: English writes the sound /ʃ/ with two letters, sh. Dutch writes it with three, sch. Ship becomes schip, shoe becomes schoen, and sheep becomes schaap. The extra letter is spelling, not a new sound.

pattern.title: Read sch as one block
pattern.content: When you see sch at the start of a Dutch word, hear a single breathy block: sch-ip, sch-oen, sch-aap. Do not split it into s + ch. The same block appears in school, which English borrowed with a sk spelling.
pattern.linguist_note: West Germanic *sk developed differently in the daughter languages: English often turned it into sh, Dutch kept the sk-like cluster but spells it sch.
pattern.trap_note: Sch is not 'sk'. Dutch school starts with the same /sx/ sound as schip; English school kept an older sk pronunciation.

exercises.prompt: Match each English meaning with its Dutch twin (The SCH Bridge):
exercises.target_answer: het schip, de schoen, het schaap, de schouder, scherp, de school
exercises.meaning: ship, shoe, sheep, shoulder, sharp, school
exercises.explanation: These are the anchors of "The SCH Bridge": read each Dutch form through the pattern, not as a new word.

exercises.prompt: Which sentence says: “The ship is big.”?
exercises.explanation: “Het schip is groot.” is the Dutch form; the other readings bend the pattern of “The SCH Bridge”.

cues: The pattern: Read sch as one block
It means: The shoe is new.
exercises.explanation: “De schoen is nieuw.” puts the thought together the Dutch way — Read sch as one block.

diagnosis.slip: an English-shaped word order slipped in
diagnosis.cue: Sch is not 'sk'. Dutch school starts with the same /sx/ sound as schip; English school kept an older sk pronunciation.

exercises.prompt: Which English sentence is built the Dutch way?
exercises.explanation: “Het schaap is wit.” is word-for-word “The sheep is white.”. The odd English is the lesson — never a model to produce. Pattern: Read sch as one block.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
cues: It means: The school is closed.
exercises.explanation: “De school is dicht.” reuses only material taught in “The SCH Bridge” — Read sch as one block.
exercises.affirmation: You heard “De school is dicht.” — a sentence built from the lesson's own Dutch, practising Read sch as one block.

twist.prompt: One more, no safety net — say: “The shoulder is warm.”
twist.explanation: Schouder and shoulder are the same word; the sch block carries the sh sound.

summary.outcome: Read Dutch sch as one sound and recognise its English sh twins.
summary.takeaway: A spelling bridge is a free word: once you see sch, you can hear the English twin underneath.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on De Brug: SCH Spelling Gym.

schip.etymology_derivation: English ship and Dutch schip are the same word; sch is /sx/.

schoen.etymology_derivation: English shoe and Dutch schoen are the same word.

schaap.etymology_derivation: English sheep and Dutch schaap are the same word.

schouder.etymology_derivation: English shoulder and Dutch schouder are the same word.

scherp.etymology_derivation: English sharp and Dutch scherp are the same word.

school.etymology_derivation: A Latin loan shared by both languages; Dutch spells the sk sound sch.

sch_sh.name: The SCH Bridge
sch_sh.phonetic_rule: English /ʃ/ (sh) corresponds to Dutch /sx/ (sch): ship → schip, shoe → schoen, sheep → schaap.
sch_sh.historical_linguistics: West Germanic *sk stayed a sk-like cluster in Dutch, spelled sch, while English palatalised it to sh.
sch_sh.philological_note: Dutch sch is not English sh; the ch is a voiceless velar fricative. School is a Latin loan shared by both languages.
